description: WE ARE SPACEBROS, the bros who are using technology to understand our planet FROM SPACE. For the “Dancing with Synthetic Aperture Radars” challenge, we’re exploring how SAR data can reveal hidden patterns and changes on Earth. We aim to turn complex satellite data into something intuitive, engaging, and useful—combining science, creativity, and technology to build something meaningful. 🚀
summary: When Cyclone Arnab hit the Godavari delta in October 2026, cloud hid the coast from ordinary satellite cameras for days, and the radar data that could see through it was scattered across portals, logins and expert file formats. MATSYA is a free, open web interface built around NISAR, the NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar Satellite. Every time NISAR passes over the Andhra Pradesh coast, a pipeline finds the new scene, cuts out the area, measures what changed against a normal fortnight and publishes it next to official alerts (IMD, NDMA SACHET, GDACS). Two layers sit on the same real data: "What happened", a plain-language, newsletter-style update so residents, teachers and journalists know what the satellite saw; and "Data for officials and researchers", with mandal rankings and their uncertainty, histograms, the storm-eye profile, raw scene downloads and a one-page brief plus data bundle a district officer can file and forward. On 9 Nov NISAR showed about 84±24 km² of likely new open water in the delta, more than ten times a normal fortnight, with 8 mandals probably flooded. Cyclone Arnab is the first event in the archive, not the product: the method works for coastal flooding in general, and adding a new stretch of coast is one config entry.
details:
WHY WE BUILT IT
Cyclone Arnab formed on 24 Oct 2026 and crossed the Andhra Pradesh coast in the early hours of 28 Oct (IMD). For days, cloud blocked optical satellites. NISAR's L-band radar kept imaging through it: the storm's eye over the Bay of Bengal on 27 Oct, and the Godavari delta 4 hours and 12 days after landfall. But to use those images, a district officer would need an Earthdata/Bhoonidhi login, multi-gigabyte HDF5 files, radar expertise and a separate check of the official alerts. The storm was the trigger. The problem is general: the people who need satellite evidence spend their time on portals instead of on the decision, and the public rarely hears what the satellites saw.

WHAT IT DOES
One interface, two layers built on the same real data.
- What happened (public): each radar pass becomes a short, plain-language update, like a newsletter: what changed since the last pass and against a normal fortnight, a few big numbers with their uncertainty, "Find your mandal", the next expected pass, an events archive, and a clear line that this is not an official warning, with links to IMD, APSDMA and SACHET. Updates are also published as JSON and Atom feeds.
- Data for officials and researchers: mandals ranked by likely new open water with +/- error, flooded area, change against normal and a sparkline across passes; radar images for every date side by side; brightness histograms with the water threshold drawn on; the storm-eye profile; the sea difference map; scene downloads with checksums and a "Cite this" button; and, for any pass, a one-page printable brief plus a zip of the data (CSV, GeoJSON, findings, README) that a district officer can file and forward.
- Shared: a map of the newest layers, a timeline of every pass, before/after swipe, permalinks and "Save this day", and an alerts strip (GDACS live, NDMA SACHET snapshot) filtered to Andhra Pradesh. Every layer shows its date, source, credit and one line on what it cannot show.

HOW IT WORKS
A Python pipeline, set up to run daily as a GitHub Action, searches NASA CMR for new NISAR L2 GCOV scenes over the configured tracks, streams only the study area from ASF DAAC with HTTP range requests (never whole files), writes compact HDF5 subsets, builds map images and statistics, writes one findings file per pass and turns the numbers into text with fixed templates (no AI model at run time). Tests gate every publish. The site is static (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Leaflet) on GitHub Pages, so it costs nothing to run. Areas, tracks, baselines and alert keywords live in one config file, so a new stretch of coast is one entry. Events (cyclones and floods) are drafted from GDACS and only shown once reviewed.
Method: coast scenes (track 55, HH and HV, 20 m) are compared with a baseline of two pre-storm passes (4 and 16 Oct). A pixel is "likely new open water" when it drops below a water threshold (-12.3 dB HH, Otsu) and both HH and HV fall by more than 3 noise sigmas. The same rules on a normal fortnight give the false-alarm level, and repeating at 2 and 4 sigma gives the uncertainty.

WHAT NISAR SHOWED (real data, no samples)
- Sea, 27 Oct: the sea was about 4 dB brighter in VV than on the calm 15 Oct pass, back to normal by 8 Nov. We located the calm eye at 16.23 N, 82.54 E, radius 6.4 ± 0.5 km, about 10 km from IMD's interpolated position.
- Delta, 9 Nov: about 84 ± 24 km² of likely new open water, more than ten times a normal fortnight (about 2 km2); 8 mandals probably flooded. This also includes Cyclone Murasu (1-3 Nov) and the Godavari river peak, and the page says so.
- Delta, 28 Oct (4 hours after landfall): no clear change.

HONEST LIMITS
L-band and S-band are not aligned at same time and position. The baseline scenes are provisional products. No ground truth. The wet-crops class did not separate from normal field change, so headlines use open water only. No wind speed is derived from radar, and nothing is a forecast or an official warning.

WHO IT HELPS AND IMPACT
District disaster cells and agriculture and fisheries officers of Konaseema, West Godavari and Kakinada: which mandals to survey first, with a brief they can act on. Cyclone researchers: a time-stamped surface view of the eye. Residents, teachers and journalists: what the radar saw, in plain words, so awareness grows with every pass.

WHAT IS CREATIVE
It treats each satellite pass as news: the same numbers feed a public newsletter and a professional workspace, with uncertainty shown in both. It runs itself, costs nothing to host, and every claim carries its source and its limit. Also it involved processing SAR data in the sea as well as on land, a field that is very less discussed and implemented.

TOOLS
Python (h5py, numpy, pyproj, Pillow, shapely), GitHub Actions, GitHub Pages, HTML/CSS/JavaScript, Leaflet, Esri World Dark Gray basemap. Code: https://github.com/Guneesh922/spacebros-nisar

USE OF AI
We used Claude (Anthropic), mainly through Claude Code agents, to plan, write and review most of the code, research data sources and licences, and draft documentation, UI text and this text. No AI generated or altered any image, map or number: maps and statistics are computed from NISAR files and the listed sources by our scripts. No NASA logo or branding is used or modified. The team chose the problem, area, users and scope, ran the logins, checked outputs against sources and is responsible for the claims.
